Baby oil. Tanning beds. Lying out for hours with no sunscreen because nobody told us how bad it really was.

It felt glamorous at the time. Everyone was doing it. The darker you were the better you looked. That's what we believed.

Fast forward thirty years and my back tells the whole story.

Sun spots. Dark patches I can't cover. Texture that feels rough and leathery in places. Skin that looks decades older than the rest of me.

And that's just what I can see with my own eyes. A UV scan showed me what's really going on underneath and it was honestly terrifying. Damage I didn't even know was there. Layers and layers of it just sitting below the surface waiting to show up.

I've carried so much guilt about it. I did this to myself. Every single session in that tanning bed, every single afternoon baking in the sun with nothing on my skin. I can't undo that.

But I can take care of what's here now.

I started using Besque Magic Body Oil on my back, shoulders, and chest every night. The areas that took the worst of it. And I wasn't expecting much because I figured this kind of damage was permanent.

But my skin started to change. Not overnight. Gradually. 

The rough, dry texture started to soften. The skin that felt almost leathery started to feel like soft again. It looked less dull, less tired, more nourished. Like it was finally getting something it had been missing for a very long time.

Seven cold-pressed botanical oils that absorb deep and help repair what years of UV exposure broke down. Rosehip for tone and texture. Vitamin E to protect and restore. Evening Primrose to rebuild what the sun took away.

body:
“Mom, people keep asking if you’re dying.”

That was my daughter… pointing at the bruises on my arms in the baby shower photos.

If your family has started treating those marks like a warning... this is going to hit hard.

So two weeks ago, my youngest called.

She wanted to bring her sister over to “talk about Mom’s arms.”

I made a pot of coffee. Set out the lemon loaf I bake when they visit.

Then they sat me down at my own kitchen table and spread those prints next to the sugar bowl.

Sick.

They actually used that word.

I just sat there.

Staring at my own hands in a stack of photos from a party I hosted.

Because I could see what they were seeing.

Those purple marks that show up if I bump the dishwasher...

Skin so thin and papery the veins look drawn on...

And the cardigan I wore in July so nobody at that shower would stare.

I told them I’d make a doctor appointment.

But honestly? I already knew what a doctor was going to say.

“It’s just aging. Thin skin. Be careful.”

I’d heard THAT speech before.

I had already tried everything they tell women my age to slather on.

Those drugstore firming lotions that feel nice for an hour and then the papery look comes right back...

The retinol body cream that made my chest sting and still left my arms looking the same in photos...

Even that expensive crepey cream kit I paid $79 for.

Nothing reached past the surface.

My arms just kept looking more fragile.

Then my friend Connie came by the next afternoon.

She’s a retired nurse. She could tell I’d been crying into that same lemon loaf.

So I told her everything.

She pulled up an article from American Body Journal.

Claire Bennett. The one ranking the Top 5 Body Firming Options women over 45 are actually comparing in 2026.

At first I didn’t want to read it.

A ranking. For skin that bruises if I hit the dishwasher.

Come on.

I was too embarrassed.

But Connie insisted I skip straight to #1.

Apparently ordinary firming lotions never fix aging body skin because they sit on top as a film... while the #1 bottle is a 7 oil press that actually goes in.

Arms. Chest. Neck. Thighs. The places that tell on you before your face does.

So I figured, what did I have to lose?

Connie is 71 and wears short sleeves to church without thinking twice.

The first week my arms just felt less papery when I dried off after the shower...

By week two those ugly marks weren’t blooming every time I carried groceries in...

A month later I went to Kroger in a short sleeve and nobody used that soft, worried voice on me.

I made myself a promise the afternoon my girls spread those photos across my table.

I was NOT going to spend the rest of my life explaining that I am not dying... just because another firming lotion sat there and did nothing.

That promise is the only reason I stopped hiding my arms.

Because without it... I would’ve booked the appointment they wanted and let them keep treating me like a patient in my own kitchen.

I’m NOT ready to be talked about like that.

And if you’re reading this... I don’t think you are either.

Should I tell them it was the #1 on that list?

Or let them keep thinking some doctor saved me?

P.S. If you want to see the Top 5 list Connie sent me, I’ll link it below.

body:
My daughter got engaged last October. I'm 61, I've been a widow for six years, and I'd been waiting for this a long time.

I'm not going to use the other mother's real name. Let's call her Pam. She's 58. Tennis three mornings a week, and the kind of arms you get from tennis three mornings a week. She offered to organise the mothers' side of things and I let her, because I was grateful someone with that much energy wanted to.

In March she sent us both the same dress in two colours. Sleeveless, floor length, for the mothers' photo the photographer takes before the ceremony. Hers in navy, mine in sage.

Then a second package came. A bolero. Cropped little jacket, sage to match. The card said, for the photos, so we don't have to worry about anything.

I stood in my kitchen holding it for a long time, because I knew exactly what she meant. My arms haven't been in a photograph since about 2011. I've got the skin above the elbow that folds like tissue when I lift my hand to my face. Papery, crepey, whatever you call it. You know the word if you've got it. I wore cardigans to my husband's funeral in July.

I looked the bolero up online. $340.

I called my daughter that night and asked if Pam had spoken to her about a jacket. She went quiet, and then she said, Mum, it's just for the photos, you'll be more comfortable.

That's the part that got me. Not Pam. My own daughter had looked at my arms and agreed with her.

I didn't argue. I said fine, hung up, and sat on the edge of the bed with the bolero on my lap. The wedding was in seven weeks.

What I did next wasn't dignified and I'll be honest about it. I went to two department stores and a pharmacy over four days and bought everything with the word firming on it. A body butter, two lotions, a caffeine cream that promised tightening, a retinol body lotion, a collagen powder for my coffee, a dry brush. Seven things. I added the receipts up later. $214.

I did all of it twice a day for two weeks and turned my arm to the bathroom light every single morning. Nothing changed. My arms felt lovely for about an hour after the shower and by lunchtime they were tight and dry again and I was reaching for the lotion a second time.

I tried the dress on with the bolero over it in the spare room mirror and it looked like exactly what it was. An old woman being hidden.

I've been going to the same pool class at the Y for four years. Tuesdays and Thursdays at nine. It's mostly women my age and we know each other's names and nothing else about each other.

There's a woman I'll call Denise. She's 63 and she's been in that class longer than I have. What I'd noticed about Denise for years was that she wore a swimsuit with no cover-up and never seemed to give it a thought. Her arms looked like arms. Not tennis arms. Just skin that fit her.

I'd never asked her about it. You don't.

The Tuesday after the fitting I was standing at the edge of the pool with my towel round my shoulders the way I always do, and she said, you're quiet today. I said my daughter's getting married. She said, that's a face for a funeral, not a wedding.

I don't know why I told her. The dress, the jacket, the $340, the phone call, all of it. She listened the whole way through and then she asked me one question.

How many products are you using on your arms right now?

I had to count them. Seven.

And how many of those are creams or lotions?

Six.

She said, that's your problem. My arms used to do exactly what yours do.

I said, used to?

She laughed and said yes, used to, come here.

She dried her hands and started digging in her gym bag, and while she was looking she explained it to me the way nobody at any beauty counter ever had.

She said, think of a plant that's gone dry. The soil's compacted and it's pulled away from the sides of the pot. You pour water in the top and what happens? It runs straight down the gap and out the bottom. The roots never get any of it. That's what lotion does on skin like ours. Lotion is mostly water. You rub it in, it feels wonderful, and within the hour the water has evaporated and taken some of your own moisture with it. So you put more on. That's why you're reaching for it at lunch.

I said, so what do you use?

She said, you stop watering the top and you feed the soil. And she put a small amber bottle with a gold pump in my hand.

She said it's oil. Seven of them, cold-pressed, so they're still whole. Oil doesn't evaporate. It sinks into the skin and stays there, which is the one thing none of my six lotions could do. One pump after the shower, on dry skin, and that's the entire routine.

I said, one thing? She said, one thing.

She'd been using it about a year. She told me the first week she nearly gave up because nothing happened at all. The second week the tight feeling after her shower simply wasn't there. By the fourth week she wore a sleeveless top to her grandson's christening and her sister asked if she'd lost weight. She hadn't.

She said keep that one, I've got two at home. Then she got in the pool and we did the class and she never mentioned it again.

I used it that night. It absorbed in about a minute and my arms weren't greasy afterwards, which surprised me, because I'd assumed oil would be. I didn't throw the other six out. I just stopped using them.

Week one, nothing I could see. I nearly went back to the caffeine cream.

Week two, I was making lunch on the Thursday and realised I hadn't thought about my arms since the shower. I checked. They weren't tight. That had never happened.

Week three, bathroom light, arm up, the way I'd done every morning for years. The skin above the elbow gathered less. Not gone. Less.

Week five, I put the sage dress on in the spare room with no jacket over it and stood there a while.

Week six was the final fitting. The seamstress, who'd seen me in that dress back in March, asked what I'd been doing because my arms looked different. I told her, honestly, one bottle of oil. She wrote the name down.

The wedding was June 14th. It was 91 degrees by the time they took the mothers' photo.

I wore the dress with no bolero. It was in my bag in case I lost my nerve and I didn't need it.

Pam arrived in the navy with a little navy wrap over her shoulders. She'd had a spray tan two days before and I think it had streaked, because she kept that wrap on through the photo and most of the ceremony in that heat.

The photographer took the two of us, then me with my daughter, and when she'd finished she said, your arms are going to look lovely in these. I said thank you like it was a normal thing for someone to say to me.

My daughter's friend, who does something on TikTok I don't really understand, stopped me at the reception and asked what I'd had done. I said nothing, just an oil. She made me spell it and typed it into her phone.

So for anyone who skipped to the end, here it is plainly.

Lotion is mostly water. Water leaves. That's why your arms feel fine at nine and tight by lunch, and it's why a drawer full of firming creams never held.

What Denise gave me is called Besque Magic Body Oil. Seven cold-pressed oils. Sweet almond, rosehip, evening primrose, vitamin E, geranium, lavender and patchouli. Pure and unrefined, so they go into the skin and stay there instead of sitting on top of it. One pump a day after your shower and that's all it is.

Over half a million women use it. It ships from the UK with free shipping and duties included.

It's at besque.co/products/magic-body-oil. Get the 200ml XL. It's 35% off there and it's the one I'd tell anyone to start with, because the small bottle went in two weeks for me. Dry skin drinks it.

One warning. There are fakes in the same bottle on Amazon and marketplace sites. Besque only sells on their own site, so that link is the only place you'll get the real one.

Pam and I are not friends. We're civil, because we share grandchildren now.

She texted me in August, three weeks after the wedding, asking what I'd used on my arms and whether the discount was still on.

I sent her the link. I didn't mention the 35% had ended the week before.

body:
My daughter got engaged last October. I'm 61, I've been a widow for six years, and I'd been waiting for this a long time.

I'm not going to use the other mother's real name. Let's call her Pam. She's 58. Tennis three mornings a week, and the kind of arms you get from tennis three mornings a week. She offered to organise the mothers' side of things and I let her, because I was grateful someone with that much energy wanted to.

In March she sent us both the same dress in two colours. Sleeveless, floor length, for the mothers' photo the photographer takes before the ceremony. Hers in navy, mine in sage.

Then a second package came. A bolero. Cropped little jacket, sage to match. The card said, for the photos, so we don't have to worry about anything.

I stood in my kitchen holding it for a long time, because I knew exactly what she meant. My arms haven't been in a photograph since about 2011. I've got the skin above the elbow that folds like tissue when I lift my hand to my face. Papery, crepey, whatever you call it. You know the word if you've got it. I wore cardigans to my husband's funeral in July.

I looked the bolero up online. $340.

I called my daughter that night and asked if Pam had spoken to her about a jacket. She went quiet, and then she said, Mum, it's just for the photos, you'll be more comfortable.

That's the part that got me. Not Pam. My own daughter had looked at my arms and agreed with her.

I didn't argue. I said fine, hung up, and sat on the edge of the bed with the bolero on my lap. The wedding was in seven weeks.

What I did next wasn't dignified and I'll be honest about it. I went to two department stores and a pharmacy over four days and bought everything with the word firming on it. A body butter, two lotions, a caffeine cream that promised tightening, a retinol body lotion, a collagen powder for my coffee, a dry brush. Seven things. I added the receipts up later. $214.

I did all of it twice a day for two weeks and turned my arm to the bathroom light every single morning. Nothing changed. My arms felt lovely for about an hour after the shower and by lunchtime they were tight and dry again and I was reaching for the lotion a second time.

I tried the dress on with the bolero over it in the spare room mirror and it looked like exactly what it was. An old woman being hidden.

I've been going to the same pool class at the Y for four years. Tuesdays and Thursdays at nine. It's mostly women my age and we know each other's names and nothing else about each other.

There's a woman I'll call Denise. She's 63 and she's been in that class longer than I have. What I'd noticed about Denise for years was that she wore a swimsuit with no cover-up and never seemed to give it a thought. Her arms looked like arms. Not tennis arms. Just skin that fit her.

I'd never asked her about it. You don't.

The Tuesday after the fitting I was standing at the edge of the pool with my towel round my shoulders the way I always do, and she said, you're quiet today. I said my daughter's getting married. She said, that's a face for a funeral, not a wedding.

I don't know why I told her. The dress, the jacket, the $340, the phone call, all of it. She listened the whole way through and then she asked me one question.

How many products are you using on your arms right now?

I had to count them. Seven.

And how many of those are creams or lotions?

Six.

She said, that's your problem. My arms used to do exactly what yours do.

I said, used to?

She laughed and said yes, used to, come here.

She dried her hands and started digging in her gym bag, and while she was looking she explained it to me the way nobody at any beauty counter ever had.

She said, think of a plant that's gone dry. The soil's compacted and it's pulled away from the sides of the pot. You pour water in the top and what happens? It runs straight down the gap and out the bottom. The roots never get any of it. That's what lotion does on skin like ours. Lotion is mostly water. You rub it in, it feels wonderful, and within the hour the water has evaporated and taken some of your own moisture with it. So you put more on. That's why you're reaching for it at lunch.

I said, so what do you use?

She said, you stop watering the top and you feed the soil. And she put a small amber bottle with a gold pump in my hand.

She said it's oil. Seven of them, cold-pressed, so they're still whole. Oil doesn't evaporate. It sinks into the skin and stays there, which is the one thing none of my six lotions could do. One pump after the shower, on dry skin, and that's the entire routine.

I said, one thing? She said, one thing.

She'd been using it about a year. She told me the first week she nearly gave up because nothing happened at all. The second week the tight feeling after her shower simply wasn't there. By the fourth week she wore a sleeveless top to her grandson's christening and her sister asked if she'd lost weight. She hadn't.

She said keep that one, I've got two at home. Then she got in the pool and we did the class and she never mentioned it again.

I used it that night. It absorbed in about a minute and my arms weren't greasy afterwards, which surprised me, because I'd assumed oil would be. I didn't throw the other six out. I just stopped using them.

Week one, nothing I could see. I nearly went back to the caffeine cream.

Week two, I was making lunch on the Thursday and realised I hadn't thought about my arms since the shower. I checked. They weren't tight. That had never happened.

Week three, bathroom light, arm up, the way I'd done every morning for years. The skin above the elbow gathered less. Not gone. Less.

Week five, I put the sage dress on in the spare room with no jacket over it and stood there a while.

Week six was the final fitting. The seamstress, who'd seen me in that dress back in March, asked what I'd been doing because my arms looked different. I told her, honestly, one bottle of oil. She wrote the name down.

The wedding was June 14th. It was 91 degrees by the time they took the mothers' photo.

I wore the dress with no bolero. It was in my bag in case I lost my nerve and I didn't need it.

Pam arrived in the navy with a little navy wrap over her shoulders. She'd had a spray tan two days before and I think it had streaked, because she kept that wrap on through the photo and most of the ceremony in that heat.

The photographer took the two of us, then me with my daughter, and when she'd finished she said, your arms are going to look lovely in these. I said thank you like it was a normal thing for someone to say to me.

My daughter's friend, who does something on TikTok I don't really understand, stopped me at the reception and asked what I'd had done. I said nothing, just an oil. She made me spell it and typed it into her phone.

So for anyone who skipped to the end, here it is plainly.

Lotion is mostly water. Water leaves. That's why your arms feel fine at nine and tight by lunch, and it's why a drawer full of firming creams never held.

What Denise gave me is called Besque Magic Body Oil. Seven cold-pressed oils. Sweet almond, rosehip, evening primrose, vitamin E, geranium, lavender and patchouli. Pure and unrefined, so they go into the skin and stay there instead of sitting on top of it. One pump a day after your shower and that's all it is.

Over half a million women use it. It ships from the UK with free shipping and duties included.

It's at besque.co/products/magic-body-oil. Get the 200ml XL. It's 35% off there and it's the one I'd tell anyone to start with, because the small bottle went in two weeks for me. Dry skin drinks it.

One warning. There are fakes in the same bottle on Amazon and marketplace sites. Besque only sells on their own site, so that link is the only place you'll get the real one.

Pam and I are not friends. We're civil, because we share grandchildren now.

She texted me in August, three weeks after the wedding, asking what I'd used on my arms and whether the discount was still on.

I sent her the link. I didn't mention the 35% had ended the week before.

body:
I found my husband in our bed with a woman from his gym.

She’s 20 years younger than me.

I didn’t scream.

I didn’t throw anything.

I looked at her.

That tight skin on the back of her legs...

That firm backside that didn’t fold when she sat up and pulled the sheet...

The kind of body I still recognized as mine, from a version of me that doesn’t live in this house anymore.

Nine years married.

And for the last year he had been distant in that polite way men get when they have already left.

No hands on my waist in the kitchen.

No looking at me when I got out of the shower.

Just “goodnight” like I was a roommate.

He saw me in the doorway.

She saw me too.

I closed the door. I sat in the car in our driveway with the engine off.

Because the worst part wasn’t even catching them.

It was that I understood why he looked.

Once I hit 56 the skin on my body just... gave up.

Crepey on my thighs if I sat down too long...

Soft and loose across my stomach in every mirror in this house...

Arms that looked older than my face by ten years.

I called Denise from that driveway.

She’s the only friend I have who works at a med spa and will not turn a crisis into a sermon.

She came over the next morning with two coffees and her phone already unlocked.

“Read this before you do something you’ll have to unsay,” she said.

It was an article from American Body Journal.

Claire Bennett ranking the Top 5 Body Firming Options women over 45 actually compare in 2026.

I almost handed the phone back.

A list.

My marriage just ended in our own sheets and she wants me to read about firming options.

Come on.

But Denise has NEVER sent me junk.

And she made me skip straight to #1.

Apparently the lotions I was living on sit on top as a temporary film.

The #1 bottle is a 7 oil press that actually goes in.

Thighs. Tummy. Backside. Chest. The places I had been dressing around.

I had already tried the drugstore firming lotions that sit there like paste...

The retinol body cream that promised bounce and left me red...

Even that specialty crepey cream system I was too embarrassed to return.

Nothing moved.

So I used the #1.

Not for him.

For the version of me that had to walk back into that house and pack a bag.

The first week it just felt different after the shower. Not greasy. Not that film I used to wipe off my legs before bed.

By week two the skin on my thighs didn’t crumple the second I sat down...

By week four I caught myself in the mirror over the bathroom sink and had to look again.

Softer, yes.

But fuller. Firmer. Like my body had come back into the room.

Six months later I ran into them at that same gym.

She was at the front desk.

He was standing there with his membership card like he still lived in our old life.

He looked at my legs first. Then the skin on my arms.

And in front of her, out loud, he said, “When did your thighs start looking like that? They didn’t look like that when you left.”

She went quiet.

Then she followed me to the parking lot and grabbed my wrist.

She thought I had a surgeon.

She begged me for the name.

Said she’d already booked a consult and she just needed to know who did my body so she didn’t waste the money.

Now I need you.

Do I tell her it was never a surgeon?

Do I send her the list?

Or do I let her keep paying a doctor for something that started with #1 on Denise’s phone?

P.S. If you want to see the Top 5 list Denise put in my hand that morning, I’ll link it below.

Just skip to #1. It’s the one they say women switch to after creams fail on thighs, tummy, and arms.

body:
The pharmacist asked if someone was hurting me.

The pharmacist leaned across the counter, lowered her voice, and asked if I felt safe at home.

I didn't understand at first.

Then I followed her eyes down to my arms.

Purple blotches, from my wrists almost to my elbows. Some fresh, some fading to that horrible yellowy green. A new one on the back of my hand that I didn't even remember getting.

"Oh, no, love," I said, and I laughed, because what else do you do. "I just bruise easily."

She smiled, but she didn't look convinced.

I walked out of that chemist with my prescription and cried in the car park.

I'm sixty-eight. For most of my life, I barely bruised at all.

Then, somewhere in my sixties, it started happening from nothing.

Brushing past the kitchen door. Putting my handbag down on my lap. Leaning on the arm of the sofa. I'd look down an hour later and there'd be a new purple patch, like someone had spilled wine under my skin.

My legs were the same. My shins. Even the tops of my feet.

And my skin itself had changed. It had gone thin and papery, dry and crinkly like tissue paper that's been screwed up and flattened out again.

I stopped wearing short sleeves. Then I stopped wearing skirts.

I'd do the shopping in a cardigan in the middle of July, sweating, just so nobody would look.

But people did look. The woman at the bus stop. The young lad at the supermarket till. I could feel their eyes going from my arms to my face, wondering.

The worst was my granddaughter.

Lily was five, and she came running at me for a cuddle like she always did. Then she stopped dead and stared at my arm.

"Nana, who hurt you?"

"Nobody hurt me, sweetheart."

She wouldn't hug me for the rest of the afternoon. She kept patting my arm very gently, like I might break.

I went home that night and sat on the edge of the bed for a long time.

I'd started to feel like I was breaking.

My daughter made me see the doctor. She ran some bloods and checked my medications, and she asked a lot of questions.

Everything came back fine. She said it's something she sees a lot in women my age, and there was nothing sinister going on.

I was relieved, of course I was.

But it didn't change how I felt when I looked in the mirror.

"Just look after your skin," she said. "Be gentle with it. Keep it well moisturised."

So I tried. I bought the thickest lotion the chemist had. It sat on top of my skin like a film, and by lunchtime my arms felt just as tight and dry as before. I tried a few more. Same thing.

Then one Tuesday at my water aerobics class, I was getting changed as fast as I could in the corner, like always, when Pat from the next locker caught my eye.

Pat's seventy-one. She rolled up her sleeve and showed me her forearm.

"Snap," she said.

A bruise, right there, just like mine.

I nearly burst into tears again, just from knowing it wasn't only me.

"Your skin looks lovely though," I said. And it did. Soft, glowing, almost dewy.

"That's the oil," she said. "My daughter-in-law got me onto it. I stopped using lotion altogether."

She reached into her bag and handed me a bottle.

"Take it. I've got another at home. Use it every single day."

It was Besque Magic Body Oil.

I read the back of it on the bus home.

Seven cold-pressed botanicals, 100% natural. No water, no fillers, no synthetic fragrance.

Evening primrose oil, rich in GLA, which helps support firmness and elasticity.

Rosehip, to help skin hold onto hydration.

Sweet almond oil, to smooth and soften.

Vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect skin from everyday environmental damage.

Then geranium, lavender and patchouli, to help even the look of skin, calm it and protect it.

It made sense. My lotion was mostly water. This was all nourishment.

That night I tried it for the first time.

I'd been worried it would feel heavy and greasy on my delicate skin. It didn't. It was silky and warm, and it sank straight in.

I smoothed it gently over my arms and hands, down my legs, over the tops of my feet. Slowly, carefully. It felt like I was finally being kind to my skin instead of just slapping something on it.

And it smelled beautiful. Soft and floral, with something warm underneath.

I kept going. Every morning after my wash, and again before bed.

After a week, the tight, dry feeling was gone.

A few weeks in, my arms felt soft. Properly soft, not that crinkly tissue-paper feeling.

My skin looked healthier. It had a glow to it, a sheen that caught the light when I moved.

My legs didn't look grey and ashy anymore. Even my hands looked cared for.

I won't pretend I never bruise now. I still get the odd one. My doctor says that's just part of my age.

But the skin around it looks and feels like mine again.

And somewhere along the way, I stopped hiding.

Last Sunday was Lily's sixth birthday party in my daughter's garden.

I wore a short-sleeved dress. The first time in two summers.

Lily ran at me, and this time she didn't stop. She threw her arms round me and said,

"Nana, you're so soft!"

I've thought about that every day since.

I'm far from the only one who's found this, either. More than 550,000 women use Besque, and it's rated 4.9 out of 5 across 20,000+ reviews.

If you've been hiding your arms too, tap Learn More to see what Pat handed me that Tuesday.

body:
I see this on nearly every woman over 40.

As a dermatologist I keep having this conversation. A woman sits down, usually over forty, and tells me she wants to talk about "a few age spots" or "a bit of crepiness" on her chest.

Then I put her skin under magnification and turn the screen towards her.

She goes quiet.

Because what she's been calling a few freckles looks completely different up close. Dense, dark clusters of pigment. Irregular patches spreading in every direction. A surface that should look smooth and even, criss-crossed and rough, like parched ground.

"Is that really my skin?"

It is. And it's one of the most common things I see in women with ageing skin.

Most of them have no idea it's there, because the mirror simply can't show it.

What they're looking at is sun damage. Not from one bad burn, but from decades of everyday exposure. The school runs, the gardening, the summer holidays, the drives with the sun streaming through the window. All the moments you'd never think of as "sunbathing."

Here's what's happening beneath the surface.

Sunlight carries two kinds of UV rays. UVB affects the top layer and causes burning. UVA is the one most women underestimate. It goes deeper, into the dermis, where collagen and elastin give your skin its firmness and bounce.

When UVA reaches that layer, it sets off a chain reaction of free radicals. I explain it to my patients like rust. Oxygen slowly eating away at metal until it weakens and flakes. Free radicals do something similar to your skin's support structure, breaking down collagen and damaging elastin a little more every year.

At the same time, your pigment cells respond to the constant exposure by producing more melanin, and over time it starts to cluster unevenly. That's what you're seeing under the microscope.

The skin on the chest and neck gets hit especially hard. It's thinner than facial skin, it's exposed most days of the year, and it's almost always forgotten when women apply sunscreen.

By your fifties, all of that starts rising to the surface. Crepiness. Dullness. Uneven tone. Spots that seem to appear from nowhere, even though they've been building for thirty or forty years.

The first thing I tell every patient is the same. Wear SPF every day, and don't stop at your jawline. Chest, neck, shoulders, the backs of your hands.

The second thing surprises them.

Stop relying on your body lotion.

Most everyday lotions are largely water, with synthetic fragrance and fillers. They sit on the surface, evaporate, and do very little for skin that's been under decades of oxidative stress. And the harsh "brightening" products many women turn to next can irritate mature skin that's already thinner and more fragile than it used to be.

What sun-exposed skin needs is consistent nourishment and antioxidant support.

That's why I so often point patients towards pure, cold-pressed botanical oils. They're naturally rich in the fatty acids and antioxidants that sun-exposed skin is running short on, and there's no water or synthetic fragrance diluting what matters.

One my patients keep coming back to is Besque Magic Body Oil.

It's seven cold-pressed botanicals, 100% natural. Vitamin E is a key antioxidant that helps protect skin from environmental damage. Rosehip is rich in fatty acids and helps skin hold onto hydration. Evening primrose oil, high in GLA, supports firmness and elasticity. Sweet almond oil smooths and softens rough texture. Geranium helps even the look of skin tone, lavender calms, and patchouli adds further antioxidant protection.

Used daily on the chest, neck, shoulders and arms, alongside SPF, it helps sun-exposed skin look smoother, more even and more radiant, and feel softer and more supple.

I'm always honest with my patients. No oil or cream will erase decades of sun. But giving your skin the right nourishment every day makes a visible difference to how it looks and feels.
